teaching.hint: After resolving all possible merges in a prefix, where can the next leftmost merge appear when one new value is included?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: A fully reduced prefix has no equal neighbors. The next mandated leftmost merge can only occur at its right boundary, and a new merged value may cascade leftward.
solution_outline.approach: Process values left to right while keeping the reduced prefix as a stack. Before adding a new value, repeatedly combine it with an equal top value, then place the resulting value after the unequal prefix.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: The stack is exactly the result of fully applying the source's leftmost-merge rule to the processed prefix, and no adjacent values in it are equal.
solution_outline.correctness: Before the next value joins, the prefix has no eligible pair. Any newly eligible leftmost pair is therefore at its right edge. Merging it may expose one earlier neighbor, so repeating the boundary merge performs the same mandatory sequence as the stated process. Induction over input values gives the exact final array.
solution_outline.complexity: O(n) amortized time and O(n) auxiliary space: each input value is pushed once, and each merge pops one value. Merged sums may need more than 32 bits.
solution_outline.pitfall: Stopping after one merge misses cascades, while merging an equal pair farther right first can change the required result.

common_wrong_turns: Make only one left-to-right pass without cascading
Choose an arbitrary equal pair rather than the leftmost
Use 32-bit storage for every merged value
source_fidelity_notes: The mandatory leftmost choice and repeated behavior after every merge were emphasized; the source examples were omitted and numeric growth was clarified.
